Kalaw Lagaw Ya, also rendered as Kala Lagaw Ya, is the primary indigenous language of the western and central Torres Strait Islands in Queensland, Australia, spoken by communities including the Gumulgal people of Mabuiag Island. What is Kalaw Lagaw Ya? Kalaw Lagaw Ya, the Western Torres Strait language, encompasses multiple subdialects associated with specific islands and communities in the Torres Strait region of Queensland, Australia. These varieties reflect geographic isolation and historical settlement patterns among the Kulkalgal, Gumulgal, and other Traditional Owner groups. Is Kala Lagaw Ya a 'western island language'? Speakers have agreed that the language as a whole should be called Kala Lagaw Ya, the 'Western Island Language'. The Western Torres Strait region, whose islands and waters lie mainly within Australia's international boundaries, includes four dialect zones, marked by broken lines on map 7.1. Where did Kalaw Lagaw Ya come from? The prehistoric foundations of Kalaw Lagaw Ya trace to the broader Pama-Nyungan language family, which encompasses the majority of Australian Indigenous languages and originated from a proto-language spoken approximately 6,000 years ago in the region south of the Gulf of Carpentaria in northeastern Australia. What is Kalaw Kawaw Ya? Kalaw Kawaw Ya is their own name for the 'Western Island Language'. Bani and Klokeid (1975 and 1976) have described the dialect of Mabuiag Island in the western central zone. The dialect of the eastern central zone is used only by older speakers; younger people have adopted Torres Strait Creole (see Shnukal, this volume) as their mother tongue.
